name: Commodity volatility flows downward: farmers and contractors absorb price swings that large producers hedge or pass through
deck: The unhedged actors at the end of supply chains—farmers, contractors, households—absorb commodity volatility that large producers systematically pass through.
core_bet: Post-2022 commodity shocks never stabilized; FY2025 results show large input suppliers (fertilizer, grain) remain profitable and returning capital to shareholders while unhedged actors at supply chain ends absorb full volatility. This asymmetry is structural, not cyclical.

mechanism: The hedging asymmetry: Large input suppliers (CF Industries, Nutrien, Mosaic) hold inventory, manage input costs, and trade derivatives to stabilize margins. They absorb commodity price swings across quarters and pass them through contracts with lead time. Farmers have no equivalent infrastructure—they make one planting decision per year with commodity prices locked weeks in advance, then absorb harvest-time volatility with no hedging mechanism. FY2025 shows this dynamic in action: CF ($1.46B earnings, $2.89B EBITDA) remained profitable even as agricultural commodity prices fell post-harvest. Farmers in the same region saw margin compression on harvested crops.

Price-pass-through cascades down the supply chain. Mondelez FY2025 demonstrates the mechanism: facing commodity input inflation, they raised prices and accepted -3.7% volume loss (mix/trade-down) rather than compress margins. Organic growth of 4.3% masks the shift—they won the price battle with suppliers and customers, but the war ends at unhedged actors. Households reduced unit purchases (-3.7% volume) to absorb price increases; farmers who couldn't raise prices (commodity-derived income) absorbed the differential. Nutrien's FY2025 results ($2.30B earnings, $6.05B EBITDA) and H1 2026 shareholder return of $848M show suppliers maintained pricing power despite softness.

Structural entrapment: Farmers have sunk costs in land, equipment, and expertise specific to grain/commodity production. They cannot exit when prices are adverse; they must continue planting. Contractors similarly face multi-year equipment debt and customer contracts that don't adjust for input cost swings. Large producers (Mondelez, CF, Nutrien) can diversify revenue, scale production, or shift input suppliers. This creates a permanent volatility sink at the farm level. FY2025's -3.7% Mondelez volume loss wasn't farmers choosing to buy less—it was households reducing commodity-derived food consumption, while farmers remained locked into production cycles.
why_now: Post-2022 volatility created a structural inflection. 2022 saw commodity shocks (Ukraine invasion, fertilizer supply disruption); 2023–2024 showed no normalization. FY2025 proved the asymmetry is permanent: (1) CF Industries and Nutrien remained highly profitable ($1.46B and $2.30B net earnings) while commodity farmers faced depressed input costs but even-more-depressed output prices. (2) Mondelez's pricing power (4.3% organic growth despite -3.7% volume) shows how large producers buffer volatility through demand-side pricing. Small producers cannot. (3) No farmer or contractor has equivalent hedging infrastructure to large firms. This is not a temporary cycle; it is a structural feature of asymmetric information and capital access. FY2025 results confirm it persists.
who_pays: Farmers absorb commodity price volatility directly through harvest-time income swings and input cost inflation. Contractors absorb it through customer squeeze (farmers cut service spending when commodity prices fall) and equipment debt still-serviced despite declining revenue. Households absorb it as food price inflation (Mondelez volume/mix -3.7% shows households reducing purchases) and reduced nutrition when commodity-derived food is unaffordable.
who_profits: Large input suppliers (CF Industries, Nutrien, Mosaic) and consumer-facing producers (Mondelez). CF and Nutrien maintained profitability and returned capital to shareholders ($1.7B and $848M respectively) despite commodity volatility. Mosaic $12.05B FY2025 sales and 10%+ global phosphate share show concentrated market power in input supply. These firms can hedge, diversify, and pass through costs. Shareholders capture the surplus.
tension: Regulatory intervention risk: If commodity price swings widen and farmer bankruptcies spike, governments may intervene with price controls, export restrictions, or subsidies (U.S. farm subsidies exist for this reason). Additionally, supply-chain risk: if too many farmers exit production (consolidation pressure), input suppliers lose customer base volume, threatening their own growth. The current system benefits large firms only if farmers remain in business and buying inputs.
surprising_part: Large producers' profitability remained uncorrelated to commodity prices in FY2025. CF Industries and Nutrien posted record earnings and shareholder returns while their end-customers (farmers) faced margin compression. This is because they control the intermediate market—pricing power in the middle of the chain allows surplus extraction upward and downward simultaneously. Mondelez's -3.7% volume loss while maintaining earnings growth shows the same dynamic: they captured value from both farmers (input supply) and households (pricing power), leaving volatility at both ends.
one_sentence: Large commodity suppliers remain highly profitable in volatile markets by hedging and passing costs through, while unhedged farmers and contractors absorb the full swing.
societal_stake: Agricultural consolidation accelerates as commodity volatility bankrupts smaller producers, concentrating farmland ownership and reducing farmer autonomy. Rural communities depend on farm income; if farmers exit, rural services (schools, hospitals, infrastructure) collapse. Additionally, if commodity prices eventually reflect true scarcity (climate, water, topsoil), unhedged producers will face existential margin compression with no institutional buffer.
